strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human responses under changing environmental feedback. Combining task representations, baseline response prediction, evidence accumulation, and reinforcement learning is a potentially useful contribution even though the components are established.

The reported prediction gains are substantive. In Table 1, numeric-input CogReact reduces MAPE from the strongest corresponding baseline's 0.3052 to 0.2703, approximately 11.4%. The video-input version also improves over comparable baselines, and adaptations achieve lower reported errors on CPC18 and PeerEdu.

The evaluation covers several input representations, component ablations, individual and group models, and leave-one-participant-out testing. The additional supervised DL+DDM comparisons are a useful effort to investigate the contribution of reinforcement learning.

The collected dataset of 21,157 arithmetic responses across four feedback regimes is a potentially valuable resource. The documented study procedure, ethics approval, and linked code/data support reuse.
weaknesses: The central DDM interpretation is insufficiently justified. Appendix A.7.1 constructs a sigmoid trajectory using SVC confidence and SVR-predicted response time, adds Brownian noise, and modifies it with PPO. The paper does not derive how this construction corresponds to established DDM parameters or validate its implied response-time distributions. Its positioning also understates conventional DDMs' ability to simulate trajectories and make predictions, weakening the claimed distinction from prior cognitive models.

The interpretability claims exceed the evidence. A reward based on terminal response-time error cannot uniquely identify the intermediate perturbation trajectory: many action sequences can produce the same stopping time. Figure 3 even shows substantial inferred 'time pressure effects' in the no-pressure group, consistent with correction of baseline prediction errors. Agreement with aggregate behavioral trends therefore does not establish recovery of cognitive mechanisms. Independent temporal validation or controlled changes to stimulus timing would be needed to substantiate the fine-grained interpretation.

The ablations do not cleanly establish why the method works. Removing DDM also changes temporal granularity, visual encoding, action scaling, and episode structure in the pure-DRL comparator. These differences complicate attribution of both accuracy gains and faster convergence to the cognitive model. Figure 11 provides useful additional controls, but a matched sequential correction baseline and comparison with a stimulus-dependent DDM would better distinguish the proposed mechanism from general benefits of temporal processing and residual prediction.

The reliability and scope of the empirical gains need stronger support. The main benchmark uses trial-level splits; participant-held-out comparisons are limited to the hybrid, pure-DRL, and SVM variants within existing intervention groups. The strongest supervised baselines are not evaluated under that protocol. The statistical tests do not explain how pairing and repeated observations within participants are handled, and training-seed variability is unreported. Table 4 also incorrectly labels the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles of individual errors as confidence intervals; these do not quantify uncertainty in the performance improvement.

The additional tasks introduce unresolved evaluation and modeling questions. Appendix A.11.1 appears to use alternative-outcome feedback to predict the same gambling trial's response time. Since such feedback ordinarily follows the choice, its temporal alignment must be specified to rule out unavailable future information. For PeerEdu, the construction and validity of sensor-derived curiosity targets are insufficiently described. Treating curiosity as a stopping-time quantity through median-based classification needs separate justification, and MAPE on targets in [0,1] requires explicit handling of zero or near-zero values.

Important reproduction details remain unclear, including the sigmoid specification, diffusion-noise scale, action discount factor, training population for the purported no-feedback SVM baseline, and the precise numeric-input CogReact adaptation that produces the best result. Smaller reporting issues also need correction: the manuscript variously reports 44 participants, 50 participants, and 36 retained participants, while the claim that every component is critical overstates Table 8, where removing the risk encoder produces no significant difference in the permutation test (p = 0.677).
